questions.q: What does .partitionBy("pickup_year", "pickup_month") do on a write?
options: Organizes the output into key=value subfolders, like pickup_year=2024/pickup_month=1/
Sorts the rows within a single output file by those columns
Splits the DataFrame into exactly two separate DataFrames
Deletes any row missing a value in those columns
questions.explain: This uses exactly the pickup_year/pickup_month columns built back in Lesson 50 — that lesson's setup pays off here.

questions.q: How does this write-side partitioning relate to Lesson 9's storage partitioning?
options: They're the same underlying idea — the exact key=value directory convention — just arrived at from opposite ends of the pipeline
They are completely unrelated concepts that happen to share a name
Write-side partitioning only applies to CSV files, never Parquet
Lesson 9's partitioning only applies to Azure, not to local PySpark writes
questions.explain: Spark's write-side partitioning and a data lake's storage partitioning are literally the same directory convention.

options: Spark skipping entire subfolders it can rule out from a filter, based on the folder names alone, without ever opening those files
Deleting old partitions to save disk space automatically
Removing duplicate values from a partition column
A process that runs only during the write, never during a read
questions.explain: Combined with Lesson 42's columnar pruning, a well-partitioned, well-filtered query can touch a tiny fraction of total data.

questions.q: What makes a good choice of partition column?
options: A column real queries commonly filter on, with a reasonable number of distinct values — not too few, not too many
Any column at all works equally well, regardless of its number of distinct values
Only numeric columns can ever be used as partition columns
The column with the absolute highest number of unique values is always best
questions.explain: Something with millions of unique values, like a raw timestamp to the second, would create far too many tiny partitions.

questions.q: Why is partitioning by year and month a classic choice for time-series data like this taxi dataset?
options: It matches how queries commonly filter (by date range) and produces a sensible, not-too-fine-grained number of partitions
Year and month are the only columns PySpark allows for partitionBy()
It's required by the Parquet file format specification
It has no real benefit over any other arbitrary column choice
questions.explain: This lets partition pruning skip irrelevant months entirely on a date-filtered query.
